To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the early events in the radiation-induced G2 checkpoint response are linked with a rapid inhibition in p34CDC2 protein kinase activity.

(1) the G2 checkpoint in response to IR is defective in ataxia telengiectasia cells; (2) p53 is not required for the immediate G2 checkpoint in normal human fibroblast; (3) immortal Li-Fraumani cells lacking p53 are defective in the G2 delay in response to IR; and (4) the G2 delay is associated with an inhibition of p34cdc2/cyclinB protein kinase activity.

the early G2 checkpoint in response to ionizing irradiation is not dependent on the presence of functional p53, but that p53 deficiency can lead to genomic instability that can result in subsequent loss of G2 checkpoint function.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the molecular mechanisms that regulate the cell cycle.
understanding the molecular mechanisms by which cells respond to DNA damage, and in particular, how these responses are defective in cells from individuals predisposed to cancer.
the molecular and biochemical mechanisms of the G2 checkpoint in normal and cancer-prone human fibroblastic cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the G2 delay in normal fibroblasts is mediated by the p34cdc2 kinase and is independent of p53, while the G2 delay observed in cells with p53 mutations is due to a defect in p34cdc2 regulation.
the early events in the IR-induced G2 checkpoint response in diploid NHFs are mediated by a p34CDC2 kinase-dependent mechanism, and that p53 is not involved in this response.
the early G2 checkpoint events are not dependent on p53 function, but that subsequent genetic alterations can result in defective checkpoint function in p53-deficient cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
p53 is required for the long-term maintenance of the G2 checkpoint function but is not involved in the early G2 delay in response to ionizing irradiation.

in normal diploid human fibroblastic cell cultures, the early events in the gamma-radiation-induced G2 delay are associated with the inhibition of histone H1 protein kinase activity, and that this early response to IR is dependent upon the presence of functional p53 protein.
p53 is not required for a G2 delay following IR, but it is required to maintain genomic stability and to prevent a subsequent G2 checkpoint defect.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the G2 checkpoint is defective in cells with defective G2 checkpoint.
the p34CDC kinase complex is the primary target for the immediate inhibition of the G2 checkpoint.
p53 is not required for the early G2 checkpoint events in response to IR.
